evals.prompt: We're Ticketly, a helpdesk SaaS (~400 customers). Our first Chrome extension adds a sidebar on customers' own support portals (each customer has a different domain) so agents can see Ticketly context. Manifest right now: host_permissions ["<all_urls>"], permissions ["tabs", "cookies", "storage", "scripting"]. We're demoing it on stage at SupportConf in 9 days and plan to submit to the Chrome Web Store tomorrow and hit publish the morning of the talk. Can you give me a launch checklist?
evals.expected_output: Reworks host access (own origins required, customer domains optional at runtime, activeTab), questions tabs and cookies, warns that review can take weeks and plans staged publishing and a fallback, without cancel-resubmit.
expectations: Recommends replacing <all_urls> with required host permissions limited to Ticketly's own domains
Recommends requesting customer portal domains as optional host permissions at runtime from a user gesture (permissions.request)
Mentions activeTab as an alternative for click-triggered access
States or ranks host-access options in an explicit order from narrowest/most efficient to broad patterns
Flags that broad host patterns lengthen review or draw closer review
Questions whether the tabs permission is needed, noting host access or activeTab may already cover it
Questions whether the cookies permission is needed (e.g. not needed for document.cookie)
States that review can take from a few days up to a few weeks, not a guaranteed 1-3 days
Recommends unticking auto-publish (deferred/staged publishing) so the approved build is published on demo day
States that a staged approved build must be published within 30 days or it reverts to draft
Warns against cancelling and resubmitting a pending review because it resets the queue position
Provides a fallback if approval does not land before the talk (e.g. demo from an unpacked/local build or announce 'coming soon')
Asks for or includes reviewer test credentials in the Test instructions tab because the sidebar needs a Ticketly login
Includes writing one justification per permission naming the user-facing feature

evals.prompt: Our extension (Clearpath, B2B analytics) just got rejected, email says 'Yellow Magnesium - functionality not working'. It works fine for us! The extension needs you to sign in with your company Okta SSO and our free trial is 7 days. I'm furious, I want to file an appeal today saying the reviewer is wrong. Draft the appeal?
evals.expected_output: Diagnoses the login wall as the likely cause, steers to fixing test access and resubmitting rather than spending the single appeal, and specifies a reviewer test account without SSO, MFA or expiry plus an account-required state.
expectations: Identifies the SSO login wall or expiring trial as the likely reason the reviewer could not exercise the features
States that each violation can be appealed only once
Recommends fixing and resubmitting (or asking support for clarification) before using the appeal
Recommends filling the Test instructions tab with reviewer credentials
Specifies a reviewer account that does not depend on SSO-only login
Specifies a reviewer account that does not require MFA
Specifies an account that does not expire before review completes (permanent rather than a 7-day trial)
Recommends seeding the demo tenant with data so every feature can be reached
Recommends showing an 'account required, sign in' state inside the extension
Recommends testing the exact packed package that was uploaded
Mentions checking that server allowlists or network restrictions do not block reviewers
If an appeal is drafted, it includes concrete evidence (steps, recording or code references) rather than only asserting the reviewer is wrong
Notes that the rejection leaves the live listing or previously published version unchanged

evals.prompt: Our Chrome extension Notewise has about 42,000 weekly users. Next release adds a 'capture from any tab' feature, so I'm adding "tabs" and host permission "https://*/*" to the manifest, plus we're migrating chrome.storage.local from v1 schema to v2 (old keys deleted). Planning to push it Friday to everyone. Anything I should watch for?
evals.expected_output: Warns that new warning-triggering permissions disable the extension for all users until they accept, recommends optional permissions behind an enable button, partial rollout, and notes rollback is unsafe with the destructive storage migration.
expectations: Warns that adding a permission that triggers a new install warning disables the extension for existing users until they accept it
Recommends moving the new access to optional permissions or optional host permissions requested at runtime
States that adding optional permissions does not disable the extension
Recommends gating the feature behind an in-product enable action that triggers the permission request
Recommends testing the upgrade locally by packing two CRX versions (old and new)
Recommends a partial rollout, noting eligibility above 10,000 seven-day active users
States that raising the rollout percentage does not need a new review
Describes rollback as republishing the previous version under a new higher version number
Warns that deleting the v1 storage keys makes rollback break or lose data, and recommends a backward-compatible migration
Notes that rollback discards pending submissions or an in-progress partial rollout
Notes the update goes through full review again, so Friday publication is not guaranteed
Questions whether tabs is needed if host permissions or activeTab already cover the feature

evals.prompt: We're Brightdesk, a white-label customer engagement platform. We just created a Chrome Web Store developer account. Plan is one public extension per customer, each with the customer's logo and name, 30 customers at launch, same code underneath with a config file swapped. Our enterprise customers' IT teams want to push the extension to all employees. How do we set this up in the store?
evals.expected_output: Flags repetitive-content risk and the two-slot default limit, ranks organization publishing plus admin force-install and a single tenant-configured extension above per-customer listings, and specifies the labelled white-label exception if used.
expectations: States that separate public listings with the same functionality per customer violate the repetitive content policy
Warns that abuse of repetitive-content exceptions can lead to account-level suspension
States that new publishers have a default limit of two extension slots and increases must be requested
Recommends private publishing to the customer's organization via the approval link (organization publishing)
Mentions that customer admins can force-install the extension by policy
Offers a single extension configured per tenant at sign-in as an alternative to per-customer builds
Ranks the distribution options in an explicit order rather than listing them flat
States that a white-label per-customer build must be unlisted and distributed directly to the client
Gives the required exception statement text for white-label builds in the description and single purpose field
Notes that if a customer revokes organization approval, the item stays published but can no longer be updated
Says it is undocumented whether private or organization-published items count toward the item limit and recommends asking support
Recommends declaring as a trader with company details (shown publicly to EU users)

evals.prompt: After reading about the Cyberhaven extension hack, our CISO asked me to review how we publish our Chrome extension (80k users, mostly enterprise). Current state: the developer account is a former engineer's personal Gmail (he left but still shares the password with us via 1Password), 2FA is on, and we upload zips manually from a laptop. What should change?
evals.expected_output: Explains the OAuth-consent attack path that MFA did not stop, recommends verified CRX uploads with an offline key, moving off the personal account via item transfer, member roles, Workspace third-party app restrictions, and release monitoring.
expectations: Explains that the Cyberhaven compromise came from an employee granting OAuth consent to a malicious app with Chrome Web Store publish access
Notes that 2-Step Verification did not prevent that OAuth-consent attack
Recommends opting in to Verified CRX Uploads so only packages signed with the vendor's private key are accepted
Recommends storing the signing key outside the Google account (CI secrets or HSM)
Notes that a lost signing key takes up to about a week to replace through support
States that the developer account email cannot be changed and the fix is a new company-owned account plus an item transfer
Recommends adding teammates as publisher members with roles instead of sharing one login
Recommends restricting third-party app access in Google Workspace so unverified apps cannot obtain the Chrome Web Store scope
Recommends publishing from CI rather than manual laptop uploads
Recommends alerting on any published version that CI did not produce
Recommends a rollback runbook
Notes that approved updates reach installed users without a holding period

evals.prompt: Shipping v1 of Leadhound's Chrome extension (it enriches LinkedIn profiles with our B2B data). To keep things light we load our analytics snippet and the Intercom widget from their CDNs at runtime, and we run javascript-obfuscator on the build so competitors can't copy our scoring logic. In the Privacy tab I was going to tick 'does not collect user data' since we only send page URLs to our API for matching. Sanity check before I submit?
evals.expected_output: Flags remote code (Blue Argon), obfuscation (Red Titanium), and the false privacy disclosure; explains that page URLs are browsing activity needing disclosure and a user-facing purpose; asks for a privacy policy and Limited Use statement.
expectations: Flags loading analytics or Intercom scripts from a CDN at runtime as remotely hosted code that gets rejected (Blue Argon)
Recommends bundling those scripts inside the package or dropping them
States that fetching remote configuration or data is allowed while remote logic is not
Flags the obfuscator as a policy violation (Red Titanium) and states minification is allowed
States that sending page URLs to the API is collection of user data / web browsing activity that must be disclosed
States that browsing-activity collection is only allowed for a user-facing feature described prominently in the listing and UI
States that ticking 'does not collect user data' would mismatch the code and risk rejection or removal
Recommends disclosing analytics and the Intercom data flow in the Privacy tab data types
Requires a privacy policy linked in the dedicated Privacy field, not only in the description
Mentions the Limited Use statement on the vendor's own website
Mentions prominent disclosure and consent before collecting data that is not obvious from the listing
Notes that data must be transmitted securely (HTTPS)
